subtype: Approach: announcing boundaries then dropping them at the first request [Pitfall]
passage: On Monday, Uday told the team on the group thread, "I'm offline after six from now on." He got three thumbs-up. On Tuesday at ten past six, with a client demo two days away, the manager, Shreya, sent a message: "Quick one, can you check slide twelve?" Uday's thumb hovered. He answered within a minute. On Wednesday a teammate sent a "small" question at twenty to seven. On Thursday someone tagged him at half past seven. Nobody was rude. They had simply learned that six meant "unless someone asks". By Friday Uday was back to replying at nine at night, and felt worse than before, because he had said out loud that he would not.

qa.q: Who sent the first message after six?
What was Uday feeling by the end of the week?
qa.a: Uday felt discouraged and guilty, because he had broken the limit he had announced.

qa.q: What could Uday do differently next time?
qa.a: Uday could hold the boundary the first time and offer an answer the next morning, and give the manager a phone route for real emergencies.

qa.q: How did the teammates read Uday's behaviour?
qa.a: They learned that the boundary bends when asked, so they kept messaging, without meaning any harm.

grounding: Uday announces he is offline after six but answers when the manager pings, so the team learns the boundary is flexible.

subtype: Approach: announcing boundaries then dropping them at the first request [Pitfall]
passage:
On Monday Tushar sent a cheerful message to his team group at the Hyderabad office: "From today I'm logging off at six. Family time! Please plan around it." Three hearts appeared.
At 8.15 that night, while he was helping his niece with fractions, his phone buzzed. Lalit, his manager: "Quick one, where's the vendor sheet?"
Tushar hesitated. It was just one question. He answered in thirty seconds.
Lalit replied, "Thanks! Also, can you check row 40?" That took an hour.
By Thursday, three different teammates had messaged him after nine, each starting with "I know you're offline, but..." On Saturday his sister asked why he had missed dinner again. Tushar scrolled back through the week and saw that the first person to break the six o'clock rule had been him.

qa.q: What time did Lalit's first message arrive?
What might Tushar have been feeling when he hesitated before replying?
qa.a: He was torn between his new limit and not wanting to seem unhelpful to his manager; telling himself it was just one question eased his unease.

qa.q: What could Tushar have done differently when Lalit messaged?
qa.a: He could have replied the next morning, or agreed beforehand that real emergencies come as a call, so the first test of the limit held.

qa.q: How do Tushar's teammates see his six o'clock rule by Thursday?
qa.a: They have learned it bends: they still say "I know you're offline, but..." and message anyway.

grounding: It shows a man announcing an evening cut-off and then answering his manager's first ping, so the team learns the limit is flexible and late messages carry on.

subtype: Approach: announcing boundaries then dropping them at the first request [Pitfall]
passage:
Kiran slumped into the pantry, where Vinita was stirring her coffee.
"Didn't you post 'offline after six' on Monday?" she asked.
"I did," Kiran said, rubbing his eyes. "And then Sanjay called at 7.30 on Monday about the demo."
"And you picked up."
"He's the manager! It was one time."
"Kiran, I messaged you at ten last night about the test plan. You answered in two minutes."
"Because I'd already answered Sanjay."
"Right. So the whole team saw that six o'clock means maybe."
He was quiet. "I guess I just didn't want him thinking I'm not serious."
"Everyone knows you're serious. Now they also know your 'offline' isn't real. Honestly, I'll probably ping you tonight too."
"Please don't."
"Then don't answer."

qa.q: What time did Sanjay call on Monday?
qa.a: Sanjay called at 7.30 on Monday about the demo.

qa.q: Why did Kiran pick up Sanjay's call?
qa.a: Kiran was anxious that the manager would think he wasn't serious, so the fear of looking uncommitted won over the limit.

qa.q: What could Kiran do now to rebuild the limit?
qa.a: He could restate the six o'clock rule, ask Sanjay how true emergencies should reach him, and then stop answering non-urgent pings every time.

qa.q: How does Vinita experience Kiran's broken limit?
qa.a: Vinita reads it as a sign his evenings are open, so she keeps messaging late, while also nudging him to stop answering.

grounding: It shows a man declaring he is offline after six but answering the manager's first call, so colleagues learn the limit is flexible and keep messaging.
